item.title: Lumbar Paraspinal Soft-Tissue Mobilization
clinicalUse: A patient says their back feels 'locked' after a long day standing. The visible problem might be guarded bending, not a tissue knot waiting to be crushed.
Trial soft-tissue contact as an adjunct to assessment-based movement and exercise rather than diagnosing stiffness by touch alone.
Use a repeatable functional task such as a comfortable forward bend or sit-to-stand.
patientPosition: Prone with a small pillow under the abdomen if comfortable, or side-lying when prone is not tolerated.
Keep knees, hips and shoulders supported to reduce guarding and avoid forcing lumbar extension.
therapistPosition: Stand alongside the treatment area with a broad stance, shoulders relaxed and wrists aligned.
Transfer weight gently through the arms rather than repeatedly loading a small thumb joint.
stabilization: The treatment table and pillows support the trunk; place the contact beside, not directly on, spinous processes.
Keep the pelvis stable enough that comfortable tissue movement can be controlled.
contact: Use broad palm/thenar or supported forearm contact over lumbar erector-spinae muscle mass adjacent to the spine.
Avoid direct focal pressure on spinous processes, kidneys/flanks or suspected injured tissues.
forceDirection: Slowly glide longitudinally along the lumbar paraspinal muscle region or use gentle stationary contact, staying within symptom tolerance.
Choose direction by comfort and clinically observed response, not a belief that one stroke must 'break adhesions'.
dosage: Use short, response-guided bouts (for example, 30–60 seconds per selected region) with feedback after each; there is no universal ideal dose.
Reduce pressure with highly irritable presentations and proceed to active movement rather than repeating manual work indefinitely.
steps: Record one meaningful functional task and ask about pain distribution, neurologic symptoms and clinical red flags.
Support the trunk in prone or side-lying and explain the intended comfortable contact.
Locate lumbar paraspinal muscle mass safely, lateral to the spinous processes.
Apply broad, slow, tolerable longitudinal gliding or stationary contact while monitoring guarding and feedback.
Modify pressure immediately if the response becomes sharper, radiating or unpleasant.
End the brief trial, ask the patient to stand safely, and repeat the same bending or transfer task.
If useful, practise graded trunk movement, strengthening or pacing strategies relevant to the patient's goal.
reassess: Comfort during the same sit-to-stand or bending task
Ability to participate in active lumbar exercise
mistakes: Mistaking temporary perceived tissue softness for proof of structural realignment.
Applying firm pressure directly over vertebral processes or vulnerable flank structures.
Finishing an elaborate massage without rechecking the task that mattered.
safety: Screen serious back-pain red flags and progressive neurologic symptoms before routine manual intervention.
Avoid pressure over recent trauma, suspected fracture, infection, severe osteoporosis-related vulnerability or unhealed surgery.
Stop for worsening radiating symptoms, new weakness, saddle sensory disturbance or bladder/bowel changes; urgent assessment may be needed.
item.visualCue: Broad lumbar paraspinal contact → short comfortable glide → standing bend retest → active movement.

story.title: The back that called itself 'locked'
story.scene: A chef finishes a long shift and says the low back is 'locked'. The clinician watches a careful bend and learns more about the problem in five seconds than by immediately pressing on the muscles.
story.clinicalDecision: A pillow supports the trunk; broad palms make slow, comfortable contact alongside—not directly onto—the spine. The clinician watches guarding. The chef breathes easily. Nothing needs to be 'broken up' for this to be a sensible trial.
story.retest: Back on the feet, the chef repeats the original bend. If moving feels easier, the session continues with graded practice and manageable activity instead of a prolonged search for the world's deepest knot.
story.punchline: The back did not need a locksmith; it needed a better question.
story.evidenceCaveat: The 2021 low-back pain guideline emphasizes assessment-based, multimodal rehabilitation. Manual input is an adjunct and is not evidence of structural realignment.
